entities.name: Thomas Thynne, 1st Viscount Weymouth
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Thomas Thynne, 1st Viscount Weymouth (c. 1640 – 28 July 1714), was a significant English statesman and landowner whose career unfolded during the pivotal transitions of the late 17th and early 18th centuries, a period encompassing the Glorious Revolution, the rise of parliamentary supremacy, and the expansion of the British Empire. As a prominent Tory politician, his influence extended from the House of Commons to the House of Lords, culminating in his critical role as President of the Board of Trade, where he helped shape the administrative machinery of nascent imperial governance.

Born into the powerful Thynne family of Longleat, Thomas Thynne commenced his political life as a Member of Parliament for Oxford University and later Tamworth. Elevated to the peerage in 1682 as Baron Thynne of Warminster and Viscount Weymouth, he navigated the turbulent political landscape with strategic pragmatism. Although initially a supporter of James II, he ultimately reconciled with the new regime following the Glorious Revolution of 1688, taking the oath to William III. His most impactful administrative role came in 1702 when Queen Anne appointed him President of the Board of Trade and Plantations, a position he occupied until 1705. In this capacity, Weymouth was instrumental in overseeing the regulation of England's rapidly expanding colonial commerce and addressing complex issues of colonial governance, from the American colonies to the Caribbean.
